title: Qal Qatal and Participles
description: Learn the Qal perfect conjugation and the participle patterns.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html:
The perfect, called Qatal in this course, is the basic suffix conjugation of the Hebrew verb. It states an action as a completed whole — "he killed", "she kept", "they wrote" — and is the form a dictionary normally lists. The Qatal is built by attaching person endings to the root: the simplest form, קָטַל ("he killed"), is the third-person masculine singular, and every other person adds a suffix to the base.

The participle is a different kind of form. It is built on a vowel pattern (the active participle looks like שֹׁמֵר, "keeping" or "one who keeps") and behaves partly like an adjective and partly like a noun. Where the Qatal reports a finished action, the participle describes an ongoing action or a role. Learn the Qatal person suffixes and the participle's four gender/number forms, because most reading depends on telling these two apart.

blocks.caption: The Qatal suffixes
blocks.html: The third-person masculine singular carries no suffix; it is the bare root in its Qatal vowel pattern. The feminine singular adds -āh (קָטְלָה), the second person adds -tā / -t / -tem, the first person adds -tî, and the plural adds -û or -nû. Reading the suffix tells you who did the action, which is why Hebrew can omit the separate pronoun: קָטַל already means "he killed".

blocks.caption: Participle as agent and adjective
blocks.html: The active participle names the one who performs the action, so שֹׁמֵר is "keeping", "a keeper", or "a guard" depending on context. Like an adjective, it changes for gender and number to agree with the person or thing it describes. It also takes the definite article and pronominal suffixes the way a noun does — behaviour you will see again when you study the noun phrase and the verb stems.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Do not confuse the third-person feminine Qatal, קָטְלָה ("she killed"), with a feminine participle such as קֹטֶלֶת ("killing"). The Qatal marks a completed action with a suffix; the participle marks an ongoing action with a vowel pattern. Check the vowel pattern and the ending, then decide whether the form reports an event or describes an agent.
